title: Reading News
intro: A back-to-school issue: a new Children's Laureate, a brand new prize worth £50,000, MPs asking for a library in every primary, and Biff, Chip and Kipper quietly turning forty.

items.headline: Before Mildred there was Peace at Last, and it suits a new Reception class
items.author: Jill Murphy
items.book: A Bad Spell for the Worst Witch
items.summary: The Worst Witch is still the most-read series across our schools, but Murphy wrote for much younger readers too. Peace at Last (1980), Whatever Next! (1983) and Five Minutes' Peace (1986) are read-alouds a new Reception or Year 1 class can meet in September, and Five Minutes' Peace alone has sold over five million copies. Worth knowing when the Y3s are hogging Miss Cackle's Academy: publishers turned The Worst Witch down at first, telling Murphy that children would be frightened by a school for witches.

items.headline: Biff, Chip and Kipper turn forty this year
items.author: Roderick Hunt
items.summary: Oxford University Press has published the Oxford Reading Tree since 1986, which makes 2026 the fortieth year of Roderick Hunt's stories and Alex Brychta's illustrations. Your schools logged Hunt 22 times this year, mostly the early levels. If you fancy marking it, the magic key and the four decades of children who have followed it are an easy assembly, and Oxford Owl has the free ebook library for home reading.

items.headline: The football season is back, and so is the reader who only reads football
items.author: Rob Childs
items.summary: Rob Childs was a Leicestershire teacher who coached school football, cricket and cross-country before he wrote any of this, which is why the matches read like someone has actually stood on the touchline. The Big Match books are still in print with Penguin alongside the County Cup series, and they are short, fast and built for the child who has decided reading is not for them. September is the moment they work best.

items.headline: Michael Morpurgo's memoir is out on 17 September, about the farm behind Farm Boy
items.author: Michael Morpurgo
items.summary: Down Burrow Lane is Morpurgo's account of fifty years on a remote Devon farm, the one that gave him War Horse, Private Peaceful and Farm Boy, which your schools are reading now. He and Clare moved there as a young schoolteacher and his wife and went on to welcome more than 100,000 city children through their charity Farms for City Children, which turns fifty this year too. Hachette publishes it in hardback at £20 on 17 September.

events.name: Roald Dahl Day, his 110th birthday
events.blurb: Dahl was born in Llandaff on 13 September 1916, so this is the 110th. It lands on a Sunday, which makes the Friday before the obvious day to do something about it.

events.name: Julia Donaldson's birthday
events.blurb: Born 16 September 1948, and still the safest bet in any infant classroom. Three days after Roald Dahl Day, if you want to run one story week rather than two separate things.

events.name: National Poetry Day
events.blurb: Thursday 1 October, and this year's theme is wonder. The National Literacy Trust has free classroom resources, and the day is partnered with Michael Rosen and Hot Poets on climate and poetry.

events.name: Michael Morpurgo's birthday
events.blurb: Born 5 October 1943, so he turns 83 a few weeks after Down Burrow Lane comes out. A neat excuse to put War Horse or Farm Boy in front of an upper key stage 2 class.

events.name: World Book Day 2027
events.blurb: Thursday 4 March. Far off, but it goes in the diary now because the £1 book list and the costume panic both arrive sooner than anyone expects.

general.label: Reading news
general.text: Patrice Lawrence MBE is the new Waterstones Children's Laureate, the fourteenth, announced on 7 July 2026 and in post until 2028. She is following Frank Cottrell-Boyce, and her theme is shared and sociable reading rather than solitary reading.

general.label: Reading news
general.text: The Booker Prize Foundation has launched a Children's Booker Prize for fiction aimed at 8 to 12-year-olds. The winner takes £50,000, each of the eight shortlisted authors gets £2,500, and three children sit on the panel that picks the winner. Shortlist in late November 2026, winner in February 2027.

general.label: Worth knowing
general.text: The cross-party Education Committee reported on 17 July 2026 that every state primary and secondary should have a funded library as a statutory requirement, that every child in England should get a library card at birth, and that the government should commit to a National Reading Guarantee from birth to 18.
general.source: National Literacy Trust, on the Education Select Committee report

general.label: Did you know?
general.text: The autumn term of the National Year of Reading has the theme The Community, about schools working with parents and their local public library rather than doing reading alone. The National Literacy Trust's toolkits and webinars are free, and you can join partway through.
